task.description:
REWORK 2 of the ISS-0440 fix design. CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR re-gated: item 2 (the --dir override and the AC1 demonstration) PASSED with no defects and is SETTLED -- do not touch it. Two BLOCKERs remain, both narrow. This is a truth-in-claims fix plus one safety guard; neither mechanism changes shape.

BLOCKER 1 -- THE SECOND-ORDER OVERCLAIM. Your rework correctly withdrew the Mechanism B overclaim. But the REPLACEMENT claim reproduces the same error one level down. Sections 3.5/AC1 now say 'structurally impossible to merge... because nothing bypasses CI' and 'the violation would still be caught, every time, by Mechanism A at CI, before merge.' That is FALSE as stated, and both ORCH and the validator verified it independently:
  - `gh api repos/tvolodi/letflow/branches/main/protection` returns 404 'Branch not protected'. main has NO branch protection: no required status checks, nothing.
  - PR #848, merged TODAY by this very session, has statusCheckRollup showing its two Backend gate runs as FAILURE and SUCCESS -- it was merged with a failing gate. ORCH re-confirmed this directly. That is a live counterexample in this repo's own history, not a hypothetical.
  So CI DETECTION is structural and unconditional (ci.yml:126 is a bare invocation, no if:, no continue-on-error -- that part of your claim is true and verified). CI BLOCKING A MERGE is NOT structural: it depends on the merging agent honoring the result, which is the same procedural character as the 1.3 claim you just withdrew.
  REQUIRED FIX: state the THREE tiers explicitly rather than two. (i) CI runs unconditionally -- structural, verified. (ii) A violation is therefore always DETECTED and recorded in CI output -- structural. (iii) Whether that detection BLOCKS the merge is procedural, because main has no branch protection and merges past red checks demonstrably happen. Then restate Mechanism A's guarantee in its true form: 'the violation is always detected and recorded', NOT 'the violation cannot reach main'. Correct every section that rests on the stronger reading, including AC1's own answer.
  DO NOT treat this as fatal to the design, and do not redesign anything. Unconditional detection plus two procedural enforcement points IS a real improvement over six prose-only mitigations that produced no detection at all. The design's value is not in question -- only the accuracy of how it describes itself. Say plainly what ISS-0440's title asks for ('structurally impossible') is NOT fully achievable in this repo's current configuration, and name what would achieve it (branch protection with a required status check) as out-of-scope repo administration. ORCH will file that as a follow-up issue; reference it as a known gap rather than silently leaving the title unmet.

BLOCKER 2 -- THE --dir FLAG'S OWN MISUSE SURFACE, UNGUARDED. The design never addresses two hazards its new flag introduces:
  (a) `--dir some/empty/or/wrong/dir` produces '0 violations, exit 0' -- indistinguishable from a genuine clean full-corpus run. Someone (or some agent) could run a scoped lint, see green, and believe the corpus is clean. Specify a guard. Options, none prescribed: refuse a directory yielding zero discovered files (non-zero exit, named reason); and/or always emit a loud banner naming the scanned directory and the discovered file count, so a scoped run can never be mistaken for a full one. A banner alone may suffice if it is unmissable -- your call, but justify it.
  (b) `--autofix --dir <real corpus>` is an unreviewed mass-rewrite surface. State what happens there and whether it is restricted. Note the corpus is currently CLEAN (1900 files, zero bad values), so a mass rewrite would be a no-op today -- but that is a fact about today, not a safety property.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE: item 2 is settled -- the --dir threading, resolve_dir/1's default, the byte-identical no-flag path, section 5's demonstration, and the rejected inside-handoffs/ alternative all stand as written. Both mechanisms keep their shape. The four-option verdicts, the hook rejection, AC3/AC4/AC5 and the corrected corpus figure all stand. Design only, no implementation code. Update the design in place, complete this handoff, commit both to feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903. rework_count 2 of max 3 -- last before ORCH must escalate, so make the tier statement complete and unambiguous.

result.summary:
Both blockers addressed in lib/letflow/design/iss440-handoff-status-enforcement.md, in place. Item 2 (the --dir threading, resolve_dir/1 default, byte-identical no-flag path, section 5 demonstration, rejected inside-handoffs/ alternative) untouched, confirmed unchanged by diff review. Both mechanisms keep their shape; four-option verdicts, hook rejection, AC3/AC4/AC5, corrected corpus figure all stand.

BLOCKER 1 (second-order overclaim): rewrote section 1 in full to state THREE tiers explicitly rather than two, using ORCH/validator-supplied verification directly -- re-ran both checks myself before writing: {"message":"Branch not protected","documentation_url":"https://docs.github.com/rest/branches/branch-protection#get-branch-protection","status":"404"} returns 404 Branch not protected (confirmed), and PR #848 statusCheckRollup shows two Backend gate runs, FAILURE and SUCCESS (confirmed). Tier 1 = CI runs unconditionally (structural, ci.yml has no if:/continue-on-error:). Tier 2 = a violation is therefore always detected and recorded (structural, follows mechanically from Tier 1). Tier 3 = whether detection blocks the merge (procedural, NOT structural -- no branch protection exists and PR #848 is a live counterexample of a red run merging). Rewrote section 3.5 end to end at this precision: Mechanism A delivers Tier 1+2 only, not cannot-reach-main; Mechanism B remains procedural and does not add a second Tier-1/2-strength guarantee; stated plainly that ISS-0440s own title (structurally impossible) is not fully achievable in this repos current configuration. Rewrote AC1s opening framing to match (the demonstration steps themselves, settled item 2, untouched). Fixed a leftover Tier-3-strength claim in section 1.2s closing paragraph (that word is earned by Mechanism A alone) to point at Tier 1+2 instead. Added new section 6.4 naming the Tier 3 gap explicitly as an out-of-scope repo-administration follow-up (branch protection on main with mix letflow.checks job as a required status check), with the exact verification command, so ORCH has a concrete follow-up to file rather than an implied claim. Updated section 7 item 3 (anti-patterns.md guidance) and added item 5 (the named out-of-scope follow-up) to match. Grepped the whole file afterward for every remaining structurally impossible/nothing bypasses/cannot reach main occurrence and confirmed each remaining instance is either explicitly quoting-and-withdrawing the original overclaim, quoting ISS-0440s own title as the premise being addressed, or a correctly-scoped statement of what is/is not achieved.

BLOCKER 2 (--dir misuse surface unguarded): added new section 2.1a (inserted after section 2.1, which is unchanged) specifying both guards named in the rework dispatch, adopted together with justification for using both rather than one: (a) a hard guard -- when handoff_files(dir) returns zero files AND --dir was explicitly supplied (not the default path), run/1 raises a usage error naming the directory and refusing to report a bare 0-violations success, closing the worst misreading (empty/mistyped scope silently reporting green); (b) an unconditional summary banner naming the scanned directory alongside the existing file count, present on every invocation including the default no-flag path, closing the remaining gap the empty-scope guard cannot (a non-empty but still-wrong --dir passing the empty check while still not being the real corpus). Justified adopting both: each guard closes a different failure shape, and their union leaves no --dir misuse unlabelled in the output. For (b) --autofix --dir <real corpus>: stated plainly this is a real, unrestricted mass-rewrite surface, and stated equally plainly why it is not restricted -- restricting it would reintroduce an agent-must-remember-the-safe-flags failure mode and would block the legitimate local-fix use case section 6.3 already describes. Named the three properties that make it safe despite being unrestricted (closed map touching only the status field; every fix reported by path and value, never silent; corpus-wide zero-bad-values state is stated explicitly as a fact about today, not a safety property of the flag, per the dispatchs own instruction not to conflate the two). Updated section 7 item 1 to list both new guards.

Verified no implementation code was introduced: grepped the full file for elixir/ex-tagged fences and def/defp/case/with/fn...do patterns after all edits -- 6 fenced blocks total, all balanced, all containing only @spec-style signatures, data literals, or comment lines; none contain a real function body.
